title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.
key_points: Suffrage is the right to vote in public elections.
It expanded over time — beyond property, then to women, then across race and age barriers.
Universal adult suffrage, the modern democratic standard, means nearly all adult citizens may vote.
Who is included or excluded shapes whose interests elected governments actually answer to.
content_html: Suffrage is simply the right to vote in public elections — but few rights have been fought over so hard or won so gradually. The idea that government should rest on the consent of "the people" is ancient, yet for most of history the people who could actually cast a ballot were a small, privileged group. Early electorates were often limited to property-owning men, on the theory that only those with a material stake should decide public affairs.
extra_html: The modern history of suffrage is the story of that circle widening. Property requirements fell, opening the vote to working men. Long campaigns extended it to women, often decades later. Restrictions tied to race were challenged and dismantled, and voting ages were lowered. The result, now treated as the democratic standard, is universal adult suffrage: the principle that essentially all adult citizens may vote regardless of wealth, sex, or race. Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how contested and uneven this expansion was across countries. The reason it matters so much is structural rather than symbolic: elected governments tend to respond to the interests of those who can hold them accountable at the ballot box, so the boundaries of the franchise quietly shape whose concerns a democracy actually serves.
